items.prompt_md: In interval DP, what does dp[i][j] represent for the stick problem?
options: The cheapest total to make every cut strictly between boundaries i and j
The cost of the i-th and j-th cut only
The number of cuts between i and j
The length of the piece between i and j
items.answer: The cheapest total to make every cut strictly between boundaries i and j
items.explanation_md: dp[i][j] is the optimum for the whole sub-range, composed of the two sub-ranges around the first cut plus the piece length. It is not just a length or a count.

items.prompt_md: Why must the table be filled by increasing interval length rather than by row i then column j?
options: It makes the code shorter
A range depends on strictly shorter ranges, which must already be computed
It reduces the number of split points
Python lists require it
items.answer: A range depends on strictly shorter ranges, which must already be computed
items.explanation_md: dp[i][j] reads dp[i][k] and dp[k][j] for k inside the range. In plain row-major order some of these cells are still empty when we need them.

items.prompt_md: Why add 0 and n to the sorted cuts as sentinels?
options: To make the cut count even
Because cuts must be unique
So the outermost piece has two boundaries and its length pts[j] - pts[i] is the cost of the first cut
To avoid sorting
items.answer: So the outermost piece has two boundaries and its length pts[j] - pts[i] is the cost of the first cut
items.explanation_md: With sentinels every piece, including the whole stick, is bounded by two points in the same array, so one formula covers every range.

items.prompt_md: What does the inner variable k mean in the stick recurrence?
options: The last cut made in the piece
The cut with the smallest position
Any cut outside the range
The first cut made in the piece (i, j), after which the two sides are independent
items.answer: The first cut made in the piece (i, j), after which the two sides are independent
items.explanation_md: Once the first cut splits the piece, the cost of each side no longer depends on the other, so dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] is exact. Choosing the first cut also explains the piece-length term.

items.prompt_md: For the balloon-bursting problem, why is it useful to let k be the LAST balloon burst in the range?
options: Its neighbours at that time are the fixed boundaries i and j, so the two sides become independent
The last balloon is always the largest
It makes the loop run backwards
It avoids needing a table
items.answer: Its neighbours at that time are the fixed boundaries i and j, so the two sides become independent
items.explanation_md: If k were burst first, the coins it yields would depend on whatever neighbours remain inside, and the two sides would interact. Treating k as last pins down its neighbours.

items.prompt_md: What are the base cases of the stick DP?
options: dp[i][i+1] = 0, since adjacent boundaries have no cut between them
dp[i][j] = pts[j] - pts[i] for all i, j
items.answer: dp[i][i+1] = 0, since adjacent boundaries have no cut between them
items.explanation_md: A range with no interior boundary needs no cut and costs nothing. Everything else is built from these zeros.

items.prompt_md: A student computes dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][k] + dp[k][j]) but forgets to add pts[j] - pts[i]. What happens?
options: The answer is the same but slower
The answer is exactly half the true answer
Every dp value is 0 because only the base cases contribute, so the answer is wrong
Python raises an exception
items.answer: Every dp value is 0 because only the base cases contribute, so the answer is wrong
items.explanation_md: The cost of making a cut is the only thing that adds to the totals. Without it, a table seeded with zeros stays all zeros.

items.prompt_md: What is the time complexity of the stick DP with m = cuts + 2 boundaries?
options: O(m log m)
O(m!)
O(m^3): O(m^2) ranges, each trying up to m split points
items.answer: O(m^3): O(m^2) ranges, each trying up to m split points
items.explanation_md: Each of the roughly m^2/2 ranges loops over up to m candidates for k with O(1) work per candidate.

items.prompt_md: What is the space complexity of the bottom-up stick DP?
options: O(m^2) for the table
O(m)
items.answer: O(m^2) for the table
items.explanation_md: Every pair of boundaries has a cell, so m^2 entries. A top-down memoised version would add O(m) recursion depth on top.

items.prompt_md: How does the cost of interval DP compare with trying every order of the cuts?
options: Both are O(m^3)
O(m^3) versus m! orders, because shared sub-ranges are solved only once
The brute force is faster for large m
Both are O(m!)
items.answer: O(m^3) versus m! orders, because shared sub-ranges are solved only once
items.explanation_md: The brute force reprices the same sub-pieces in many different orders. Memoising by the pair of boundaries collapses m! orders into m^2 states.

items.prompt_md: Given a rod with marked cut positions, cutting a piece costs its current length, and you may cut in any order. Find the minimum total cost to make all the cuts.
options: Greedy: always take the locally best choice
Two-sequence DP: dp[i][j] over prefixes of two inputs
Interval DP: dp[i][j] over a range, try each split k
Backtracking over every order
items.answer: Interval DP: dp[i][j] over a range, try each split k
items.explanation_md: The cost depends on the current piece, and after the first cut each side is independent. That is a range DP with a split point; greedy picks fail because order changes later costs.

items.prompt_md: A row of balloons with values: bursting one earns the product of it and its current neighbours. Choose the order that maximises total coins.
options: Greedy: always take the locally best choice
1D DP over a single index
Backtracking over every order
Interval DP: dp[i][j] over a range, try each split k
items.answer: Interval DP: dp[i][j] over a range, try each split k
items.explanation_md: Think about the last balloon burst in a range so its neighbours are fixed. It is interval DP, not greedy, because the order changes neighbours.

items.prompt_md: A convex polygon with labelled corners is split into triangles; a triangle costs the product of its three labels. Minimise the total cost.
options: Interval DP: dp[i][j] over a range, try each split k
Two-sequence DP: dp[i][j] over prefixes of two inputs
Knapsack-style DP over items and capacity
Greedy: always take the locally best choice
items.answer: Interval DP: dp[i][j] over a range, try each split k
items.explanation_md: Pick the triangle on edge (i, j) by its apex k, then the two remaining sides are independent sub-polygons. That is interval DP.

items.prompt_md: Given two strings, find the length of their longest common subsequence.
options: Interval DP: dp[i][j] over a range, try each split k
Two-sequence DP: dp[i][j] over prefixes of two inputs
Knapsack-style DP over items and capacity
Greedy: always take the locally best choice
items.answer: Two-sequence DP: dp[i][j] over prefixes of two inputs
items.explanation_md: dp[i][j] covers prefixes of both strings and moves one step at a time with no inner loop over split points. That is two-sequence DP, not interval DP.

items.prompt_md: Choose items with weights and values to maximise value within a weight limit.
options: Interval DP: dp[i][j] over a range, try each split k
Two-sequence DP: dp[i][j] over prefixes of two inputs
Knapsack-style DP over items and capacity
Greedy: always take the locally best choice
items.answer: Knapsack-style DP over items and capacity
items.explanation_md: The state is (items considered, capacity), and each item is taken or skipped. It is knapsack, not a range split.

items.prompt_md: Given a set of intervals, remove as few as possible so that no two overlap.
options: Interval DP: dp[i][j] over a range, try each split k
Knapsack-style DP over items and capacity
Backtracking over every order
Greedy: always take the locally best choice
items.answer: Greedy: always take the locally best choice
items.explanation_md: Sorting by end time and keeping the earliest-ending compatible interval is provably optimal. Interval DP would be needless cubic work; this belongs to the greedy and intervals family.

items.prompt_md: Find the least number of operations to make a string a palindrome by merging adjacent equal-cost blocks, where merging a range costs the sum of its parts and the order of merges matters.
options: Interval DP: dp[i][j] over a range, try each split k
1D DP over a single index
Greedy: always take the locally best choice
Sort and sweep
items.answer: Interval DP: dp[i][j] over a range, try each split k
items.explanation_md: Merging a contiguous range into one block with order-dependent cost means dp[i][j] over ranges, trying each split point.

items.prompt_md: Count the number of distinct ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time.
options: Interval DP: dp[i][j] over a range, try each split k
1D DP over a single index
Two-sequence DP: dp[i][j] over prefixes of two inputs
Backtracking over every order
items.answer: 1D DP over a single index
items.explanation_md: The answer for step i depends only on steps i-1 and i-2, so a one-dimensional DP is enough. No ranges or splits are involved.

items.prompt_md: Merge a row of stone piles into one pile, where merging two adjacent piles costs their combined size. Find the minimum total cost.
options: Greedy: always take the locally best choice
1D DP over a single index
Interval DP: dp[i][j] over a range, try each split k
Two-sequence DP: dp[i][j] over prefixes of two inputs
items.answer: Interval DP: dp[i][j] over a range, try each split k
items.explanation_md: Only adjacent piles can merge, so every merge acts on a contiguous range. dp[i][j] tries each split point and adds the range total. A greedy smallest-pair merge is not always optimal here.

items.prompt_md: List all subsets of a small set of numbers.
options: Interval DP: dp[i][j] over a range, try each split k
1D DP over a single index
Sort and sweep
Backtracking over every order
items.answer: Backtracking over every order
items.explanation_md: Every subset is required, not an optimum, so this is enumeration with backtracking.
